patient.chief_complaint: Sudden onset right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Jing Li is a 78-year-old right-handed East Asian woman with a history of atrial fibrillation (recently self-discontinued warfarin three weeks ago due to recurrent epistaxis), poorly controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction who was brought to the emergency department by EMS after an acute onset of right-sided weakness and speech difficulty. Her daughter reports that she spoke with her mother on the phone at approximately 09:00 this morning and she was completely normal, discussing plans for a family dinner this weekend. At approximately 10:45, a neighbor found Mrs. Jing Li on the floor of her kitchen, awake but unable to speak coherently and with her right arm and leg limp. The neighbor called 911 immediately. EMS arrived at 10:58 and documented right gaze preference, dense right hemiplegia, and expressive aphasia. A stroke alert was activated in the field. Prehospital finger-stick glucose was 204 mg/dL. The patient was transported emergently to the nearest comprehensive stroke center, arriving at 11:22. On arrival, telemetry immediately demonstrated an irregularly irregular rhythm consistent with atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 108 bpm. The patient was visibly anxious and attempting to speak but producing only fragmentary, effortful words. She was able to follow simple one-step commands with her left hand. Her daughter arrived shortly after and confirmed that her mother had stopped taking warfarin approximately three weeks ago because she was having frequent nosebleeds and was afraid of 'bleeding out.' She had not yet seen her cardiologist to discuss alternative anticoagulation. The daughter also notes her mother's blood pressure has been running high at home despite medications, with readings in the 170s-180s systolic. There was no preceding headache, seizure, recent trauma, fever, or change in baseline function prior to today's event. Last known well time is established at 09:00, approximately 2 hours and 22 minutes prior to ED arrival.

results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: For patients with AF-related stroke, initiation of anticoagulation should be individualized based on infarct size and hemorrhagic transformation risk. Generally, 4-14 days post-stroke depending on severity.

results.title: Timing of Anticoagulation After Acute Ischaemic Stroke (ELAN Trial)
results.authors: Fischer U, Koga M, et al.
results.key_finding: Early anticoagulation (within 48 hours for minor/moderate strokes) with DOACs was non-inferior to delayed anticoagulation and may reduce recurrent ischemic events without increasing bleeding risk.

results.title: European Stroke Organisation guidelines on secondary prevention after TIA and ischaemic stroke
results.key_finding: DOACs are preferred over warfarin for AF-related stroke prevention. CHA2DS2-VASc score should guide anticoagulation decisions.

output.summary: Current guidelines recommend initiating anticoagulation with a DOAC for secondary stroke prevention in patients with AF-related ischemic stroke. Timing depends on infarct severity: earlier initiation (within 48 hours) may be appropriate for small-to-moderate strokes, while larger infarctions generally warrant waiting 7-14 days. DOACs are preferred over warfarin due to lower intracranial hemorrhage risk and do not require routine INR monitoring. The CHA2DS2-VASc scoring system guides anticoagulation decisions in atrial fibrillation.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Begin secondary prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) and high-intensity statin per mechanism
Reassess anticoagulation strategy: DOAC preferred for non-valvular AF (lower intracranial hemorrhage risk vs warfarin)
Manage recurrent epistaxis (ENT consult, modifiable bleeding factors) so that anticoagulation can be safely resumed
Consider left atrial appendage occlusion (WATCHMAN) for AF patients with recurrent bleeding intolerance
Engage shared decision making to address adherence
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not leave the patient on antiplatelet alone for AF — recurrence risk far exceeds bleeding risk in most cases
Do not resume warfarin without addressing the underlying bleeding source
key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Recurrent bleeding on warfarin is an indication to switch to a DOAC (lower ICH risk) rather than abandon anticoagulation
LAA occlusion (WATCHMAN) is an option for patients with absolute contraindications to long-term anticoagulation
Patient education and shared decision making improve anticoagulation adherence and reduce recurrence
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward - sudden onset right hemiplegia and aphasia in a patient with known AF who self-discontinued anticoagulation, with clear LVO on imaging
clinical_pearls: Self-discontinuation of anticoagulation is a common real-world scenario leading to cardioembolic stroke; always inquire about medication adherence
CHA2DS2-VASc score in this patient is 7 (female, age 65-74, HTN, DM, CHF, vascular disease, prior stroke), predicting very high annual stroke risk without anticoagulation
DOACs are preferred over warfarin for AF-related stroke prevention due to lower ICH risk and no INR monitoring requirement, which may improve adherence
Poorly controlled hypertension contributes to both small vessel disease and increases hemorrhagic transformation risk after thrombolysis

case_body_concerns: Gaze-direction inconsistency: HPI ('right gaze preference') and cranial_nerves ('Conjugate right gaze deviation with forced gaze preference') describe rightward gaze, but this is a LEFT MCA stroke with right-sided hemiparesis. Cortical gaze deviation is toward the lesion — eyes should deviate LEFT (away from the weak right side). Rightward gaze is the wrong direction for a left-hemisphere lesion. Flagged for clinician adjudication (would likely correct to leftward gaze in both HPI and exam).
